section_map.summary: The Summary Sheet compresses parameters, network concepts, Voronoi and extremal optimization, 104-versus-108 placement figures, probabilistic reachability, and stated strengths and weaknesses into a one-page decision overview.

The Abstract moves from a capacity-and-interference two-tier network to weak and strong requirements, a cellular benchmark, Voronoi minimum-enclosing-circle refinement, quantitative 11 and 104 repeater results, frequency and tone assignment, and terrain or density extensions.

The Introduction distinguishes homogeneous relay research from the paper's user-repeater hierarchy, identifies coverage, placement, capacity, and interference gaps, announces a benchmark plus three algorithmic modules, and closes with a detailed section roadmap.

The problem section defines the radius-forty domain, user count, repeater receive and transmit frequencies, PL tones, a simplified interference predicate, coverage, capacity, and the required composition of a complete placement solution.

The model represents users and repeaters as two node classes in a directed graph, defines user-to-repeater and repeater-to-repeater edges, separates capacity, interference, coverage, and global reachability conditions, and proves two sufficient implication statements.

The propagation analysis derives a free-space received-power relation, converts it into a link budget, selects empirical power and threshold values, and reports repeater and user communication radii that drive all later geometry.

The capacity subsection starts from Shannon information rate, borrows a CDMA-style energy-to-noise expression, substitutes gain and voice factors, and reports a single-repeater capacity near 119 users.

The paper replaces mobile discrete users by a uniform continuous density, converts capacity into a Voronoi-area constraint, distinguishes 324 interference-free from 270 non-interacting repeater assignments, and derives geometric and capacity lower bounds.

The baseline arranges repeaters at regular-hexagon centers, tabulates small covering constructions, chooses cell edge length from coverage and capacity, and obtains 12 and 108 repeater benchmarks for the two population scales.

The main algorithm starts at an analytic lower bound, randomizes repeater locations, builds clipped Voronoi cells, finds each cell's minimum enclosing circle, moves sites to circle centers, checks feasibility, then perturbs the least-area cell or increases the repeater count.

The secondary algorithm builds a distance graph, chooses a minimum or maximum spanning tree, removes selected incident edges to create routes, assigns one PL tone per route, and chains receiver and transmitter frequencies along each route.

For an ideal repeater radius of 85.45 miles, the results report 11 repeaters for 1,000 users and 104 for 10,000, give full coordinate and frequency tables, and use a circle-covering theorem to exclude ten small circles in the first case.

With the radius shortened to forty miles, the paper keeps the same locations, changes frequency and tone routes, and estimates random ordered-point reachability at 90.71 and 97.12 percent for the two network sizes.

The sensitivity section sweeps user count and user communication radius, compares the proposed and cellular counts, and explains a transition from coverage-radius limitation to repeater-capacity limitation.

The discrete correction models the count in a Voronoi cell with a binomial law, derives its mean and standard deviation, and replaces nominal capacity 119 by a heuristic two-standard-deviation tolerant capacity of 99.

The terrain discussion proposes lower-level hollow repeaters and higher-level mountain-top repeaters, then sketches tone and frequency reuse rules intended to use terrain shielding while preserving hierarchical relay paths.

The conclusion restates the two-tier model, cellular benchmark, Voronoi extremal optimizer, spanning-tree allocation, 11 and 104 counts, probabilistic reachability, broad applicability claims, and two explicit weaknesses.

The appendices centralize parameter values, mathematical symbols, and seven assumptions, enabling cross-checks among the link budget, capacity derivation, continuous approximation, graph definitions, and claimed propagation boundary.

The references connect relay networking, circle covering, Voronoi diagrams, extremal optimization, antenna theory, CDMA capacity, and base-station placement, but include unstable web sources and no executable reproduction package.

assumptions.summary: The service region is a circle of radius forty miles with N homogeneous mobile users.
Repeater resources lie in 145-148 MHz with a 0.6 MHz duplex difference and 54 PL tones.
Same-tone repeaters within twice the repeater radius interfere when transmitter frequencies differ by less than the threshold.
Users always select the nearest repeater.
Users and repeaters can be represented as a directed two-tier graph.
A repeater radius at least the service diameter makes any coverage solution strong in the modeled sense.
The base region permits free-space fading without terrain, structures, weather, or other propagation effects.
Ideal isotropic or high-gain antenna relations provide usable communication radii.
The Utah ERP table supports a nominal 100 W repeater value.
A one-microwatt receive threshold is suitable for users and repeaters.
A CDMA-inspired gain relation can approximate narrowband repeater capacity.
Background noise and other-repeater interference can be neglected in the capacity calculation.
User locations can be replaced by a continuous uniform density and fractional local user counts.
Nearest-repeater Voronoi regions determine load.
Frequency choices at exactly 0.6 MHz spacing are noninterfering under the strict-threshold rule.
Regular-hexagon cellular layouts provide a useful analytic benchmark.
Moving sites to minimum-enclosing-circle centers improves worst-cell coverage sufficiently for iterative refinement.
The least-area Voronoi cell is the least-fit individual for extremal optimization.
Distance-weighted minimum or maximum spanning trees provide useful local-versus-wide routing alternatives.
Terrain can be handled qualitatively by hollow access nodes, mountain-top backbone nodes, and terrain-enabled frequency reuse.

results_trace.summary: The Summary Sheet contrasts the proposed 104-site layout with the 108-site cellular benchmark and reports 97.12 percent random-pair reachability.
The link-budget analysis reports R=85.45 miles and r=15.28 miles, subject to the Equation 7 warning.
The capacity derivation reports approximately 119 simultaneous users, while later bounds use 118.
The frequency abstraction reports 324 interference-free and 270 non-interacting repeater assignments.
Necessary count bounds are at least 7 geometrically, 9 for 1,000 users by capacity, and 85 for 10,000.
The cellular benchmark uses 12 repeaters for 1,000 users.
The cellular benchmark uses 108 repeaters for 10,000 users.
The proposed algorithm uses 11 repeaters for 1,000 users with reported maximum continuous load about 112.
The ten-circle theorem excludes ten ideal coverage circles, supporting an eleven-circle minimum within the stated subproblem.
The proposed algorithm reports 104 repeaters and 21 tones for 10,000 users under ideal R.
At R=40, the eleven-site plan reaches 90708 of 100000 sampled ordered point pairs, or 90.71 percent.
At R=40, the 104-site plan is reported at 97.12 percent sampled ordered-point reachability.
The two-sigma heuristic reduces nominal capacity 119 to tolerant capacity 99.

Adds extremal perturbation and repeater-count increments to escape local configurations.

Revisits the continuous approximation with a discrete load distribution and a capacity margin.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The Abstract's constraint-to-benchmark-to-algorithm-to-numeric-result sequence is judge-friendly, but the unqualified optimum wording weakens trust.
The visual Voronoi and enclosing-circle iteration makes the mechanism easy to inspect, provided randomized performance and feasibility are separately validated.
Pairing a construction with a lower-bound theorem can strongly support a resource count when every scope condition is explicit.

weaknesses.summary: The Summary Sheet is completely absent from the text layer even though it contains dense text and two result figures.
The 97.12 percent reachability headline is probabilistic, while the same page admits there is no method guaranteeing universal point-to-point communication.
The Abstract calls eleven repeaters the real optimum without immediately limiting the claim to the idealized continuous circle-covering subproblem.
The Introduction contains an unfinished comparison sentence ending with 'in the later case.'
Different PL tones do not by themselves remove same-frequency or adjacent-frequency radio interference; the paper's predicate is an abstraction.
The frequency and tone counts are regional or problem-specific resources and cannot be generalized as a universal amateur-radio plan.
Only user-to-repeater and repeater-to-repeater directed edges are explicit; bidirectional user communication needs an additional symmetry or downlink assumption.
Assigning every user to the nearest repeater can create avoidable overload when a slightly farther repeater has spare capacity.
The reachable-area definition ignores a user's own direct communication disk and therefore represents a deliberate approximation.
R at least twice Phi is a universal sufficient condition for weak and strong equivalence, not a necessary condition for every particular network.
The free-space model excludes terrain, clutter, fading, antenna patterns, diffraction, atmospheric effects, and receiver implementation losses.
Equation 5 is attributed to Shannon theory although it is the Friis free-space path-loss relation.
Equation 6 mixes quantities originally introduced in watts with a dB-domain additive budget without an explicit conversion convention.
Equation 7 uses the constant 37.2328, while Equations 5-6 and the listed gains and losses imply a value near 3.72 rather than 37.23.
Using ERP from Table 1 and then adding transmitter antenna gain risks double-counting antenna gain.
The 39 dB VHF antenna gain is physically extraordinary and is not labeled dBi or dBd.
Table 1 contains repeated call signs and an old web source but no sampling date, cleaning rule, or summary statistic.
The one-microwatt receive threshold equals about -30 dBm and is far above common VHF receiver sensitivity; a microvolt-versus-microwatt confusion is plausible.
The reported R=85.45 miles and r=15.28 miles inherit the unresolved Equation 7 arithmetic and link-budget assumptions.
Equation 8 gives information rate in bits per second, but the text incorrectly says it is measured in watt or dB.
P_ur is a received power, but the text incorrectly says it is measured in bps.
The CDMA processing-gain relation is transferred to a narrowband repeater problem without a justified air-interface model.
The paper ignores background noise and other-repeater interference while simultaneously using SNR and E_b/N_0 to derive capacity.
The conversions 39 dB=7966.40 W, 0.4 dB=1.07 W, and 18 dB=63.01 W attach watts to dimensionless ratios.
Ten to the power 0.4/10 is about 1.096, not 1.07.
Calling 18 dB the midpoint of 5-30 dB is a rounded choice; the arithmetic midpoint is 17.5 dB.
The reported capacity near 119 is a model output under disputed gain, interference, and unit assumptions rather than an equipment specification.
The continuous approximation permits fractional users and suppresses local load variability until the later correction.
The 324 and 270 limits answer different questions—frequency separation versus avoidance of inverse-pair feedback—and should not be merged.
The five-per-tone non-interacting maximum is argued informally through a pigeonhole statement rather than a complete combinatorial proof.
The statement that when R is at least Phi any pair may interfere is existential or permissive wording, not a guarantee that every pair lies within R.
The area lower bound of seven is necessary only and ignores overlap and boundary inefficiency.
Equation 16 uses C=118 immediately after Equation 12 reports approximately 119, without explaining the conservative rounding.
Several Table 2 covering radii are described as hand calculations without derivations.
The twelve-cell conclusion excludes eleven only within the chosen regular-hexagon benchmark family, not among all circle placements.
The 108-cell result is a sufficient cellular construction, not a lower bound or an optimum.
The iterative algorithm claims to seek the least number but is randomized and has no global-optimality guarantee.
The paper calls the minimum enclosing circle a circumscribed circle, which can be misleading because it need not pass through all polygon vertices.
Small total site displacement does not prove monotone improvement or convergence of the maximum enclosing-circle radius.
The feasibility step says it counts users, while the implemented continuous model appears to use density times Voronoi area.
Random seeds, independent run counts, success rates, and runtime for the extremal optimizer are not reported.
Selecting the smallest Voronoi area as the least-fit repeater does not directly target the largest radius or largest load violation.
The spanning-tree edge weights are not formally defined even though minimum and maximum trees are central choices.
The claim that minimum-spanning-tree edges do not intersect needs the geometric and graph conditions under which it holds.
For degree k greater than three, deleting k-2 incident edges leaves degree two; if the intended cap is three the count should be k-3.
The component-balance summation leaves the pair index domain and double-counting convention undefined.
A spanning tree changes relay routes but does not by itself enlarge each repeater's user coverage disk, contrary to parts of the explanation.
A node with multiple route neighbors may face incompatible receiver-frequency requirements; direction and duplex constraints are not formalized.
The weather-based reduction from 85.45 to 40 miles is qualitative and unsupported by attenuation data or a revised link budget.
The sentence using R at least Phi as the threshold for any two repeaters to interfere conflicts with the earlier diameter condition R at least 2 Phi.
The eleven-site construction is displayed numerically but the proof does not independently verify every point of the target disk is covered by the listed coordinates.
The optimality proof depends on the exact scope and correctness of cited Theorem r(n) for closed congruent circles.
The 104-site result does not report its maximum enclosing-circle radius, maximum cell load, or an executable constraint audit.
The 90.71 percent Monte Carlo estimate gives no random seed or confidence interval; an approximate 95 percent sampling margin is about 0.18 percentage points.
The 6.4 paragraph refers to a solution in subsection 6.4 itself, likely an erroneous self-reference to subsection 6.2.
Two examples do not establish that adding repeaters generally increases every user's reachable area under the route assignment.
Tables 6 and 8 provide coordinates and channel labels but no machine-checkable proof that every interference and directed-connectivity constraint holds.
Equation 18 gives a parameter-based transition near N=816 with the appendix values, so 'about 1000' is only a coarse description.
Figure 13 lacks independent-run variability, optimum baselines, and uncertainty for the randomized proposed algorithm.
The text calls X Bernoulli, but the displayed count distribution is binomial.
Normalizing each Figure 14 curve by its own maximum hides absolute repeater-count differences.
The two-standard-deviation capacity rule is heuristic and does not specify a target tail probability or simultaneous-overload guarantee.
Approximating the binomial standard deviation by the square root of the mean omits the one-minus-p factor.
A two-meter wavelength alone does not justify a strong general claim that VHF readily bypasses small mountains.
Figure 15 is separated from its caption across a page break and lacks a complete legend.
Multiple lower-tier repeaters sharing one transmit frequency and PL tone can collide on simultaneous uplinks without scheduling or capture assumptions.
Terrain shielding is proposed without path profiles, diffraction calculations, or link-budget validation.
The claim that the method is much faster than simulated annealing is unsupported by runtime tables or experimental settings.
The claim of higher local-optimum escape ability is unsupported by repeated-run success statistics.
The 97.12 percent reachability result is empirical and cannot replace the strong solution's universal reachability condition.
Appendix A leaves the information bit-rate parameter without a numerical value, even though it is needed in the printed capacity derivation.
The symbol table gives V_u and V_u-prime the same description, obscuring their intended difference.
Assumption A5 of no background noise conflicts directly with the use of SNR, N_0, and E_b/N_0.
Assumption A6 about no noisy impact from repeaters is poorly reconciled with I_other, I_self, and the explicit interference condition.
Treating fog, rivers, hills, buildings, and solar activity as one generic interference class mixes propagation loss, obstruction, noise, and fading.
Wikipedia and old web pages support important engineering statements but are unstable or weak primary evidence.
The paper provides no source code, random seeds, machine-readable tables, or complete reproduction package.

independent_extensions.summary: Rebuild the bidirectional link budget with calibrated antenna gains, receiver sensitivity in dBm, ERP/EIRP consistency, terrain and clutter loss, fade margin, and uncertainty on R and r.

unresolved_questions: The Summary Sheet is completely absent from the text layer even though it contains dense text and two result figures.
The 97.12 percent reachability headline is probabilistic, while the same page admits there is no method guaranteeing universal point-to-point communication.
The Abstract calls eleven repeaters the real optimum without immediately limiting the claim to the idealized continuous circle-covering subproblem.
The Introduction contains an unfinished comparison sentence ending with 'in the later case.'
Different PL tones do not by themselves remove same-frequency or adjacent-frequency radio interference; the paper's predicate is an abstraction.
The frequency and tone counts are regional or problem-specific resources and cannot be generalized as a universal amateur-radio plan.
Only user-to-repeater and repeater-to-repeater directed edges are explicit; bidirectional user communication needs an additional symmetry or downlink assumption.
Assigning every user to the nearest repeater can create avoidable overload when a slightly farther repeater has spare capacity.
The reachable-area definition ignores a user's own direct communication disk and therefore represents a deliberate approximation.
R at least twice Phi is a universal sufficient condition for weak and strong equivalence, not a necessary condition for every particular network.
The free-space model excludes terrain, clutter, fading, antenna patterns, diffraction, atmospheric effects, and receiver implementation losses.
Equation 5 is attributed to Shannon theory although it is the Friis free-space path-loss relation.
Equation 6 mixes quantities originally introduced in watts with a dB-domain additive budget without an explicit conversion convention.
Equation 7 uses the constant 37.2328, while Equations 5-6 and the listed gains and losses imply a value near 3.72 rather than 37.23.
Using ERP from Table 1 and then adding transmitter antenna gain risks double-counting antenna gain.
The 39 dB VHF antenna gain is physically extraordinary and is not labeled dBi or dBd.
Table 1 contains repeated call signs and an old web source but no sampling date, cleaning rule, or summary statistic.
The one-microwatt receive threshold equals about -30 dBm and is far above common VHF receiver sensitivity; a microvolt-versus-microwatt confusion is plausible.
The reported R=85.45 miles and r=15.28 miles inherit the unresolved Equation 7 arithmetic and link-budget assumptions.
Equation 8 gives information rate in bits per second, but the text incorrectly says it is measured in watt or dB.
P_ur is a received power, but the text incorrectly says it is measured in bps.
The CDMA processing-gain relation is transferred to a narrowband repeater problem without a justified air-interface model.
The paper ignores background noise and other-repeater interference while simultaneously using SNR and E_b/N_0 to derive capacity.
The conversions 39 dB=7966.40 W, 0.4 dB=1.07 W, and 18 dB=63.01 W attach watts to dimensionless ratios.
Ten to the power 0.4/10 is about 1.096, not 1.07.
Calling 18 dB the midpoint of 5-30 dB is a rounded choice; the arithmetic midpoint is 17.5 dB.
The reported capacity near 119 is a model output under disputed gain, interference, and unit assumptions rather than an equipment specification.
The continuous approximation permits fractional users and suppresses local load variability until the later correction.
The 324 and 270 limits answer different questions—frequency separation versus avoidance of inverse-pair feedback—and should not be merged.
The five-per-tone non-interacting maximum is argued informally through a pigeonhole statement rather than a complete combinatorial proof.
The statement that when R is at least Phi any pair may interfere is existential or permissive wording, not a guarantee that every pair lies within R.
The area lower bound of seven is necessary only and ignores overlap and boundary inefficiency.
Equation 16 uses C=118 immediately after Equation 12 reports approximately 119, without explaining the conservative rounding.
Several Table 2 covering radii are described as hand calculations without derivations.
The twelve-cell conclusion excludes eleven only within the chosen regular-hexagon benchmark family, not among all circle placements.
The 108-cell result is a sufficient cellular construction, not a lower bound or an optimum.
The iterative algorithm claims to seek the least number but is randomized and has no global-optimality guarantee.
The paper calls the minimum enclosing circle a circumscribed circle, which can be misleading because it need not pass through all polygon vertices.
Small total site displacement does not prove monotone improvement or convergence of the maximum enclosing-circle radius.
The feasibility step says it counts users, while the implemented continuous model appears to use density times Voronoi area.
Random seeds, independent run counts, success rates, and runtime for the extremal optimizer are not reported.
Selecting the smallest Voronoi area as the least-fit repeater does not directly target the largest radius or largest load violation.
The spanning-tree edge weights are not formally defined even though minimum and maximum trees are central choices.
The claim that minimum-spanning-tree edges do not intersect needs the geometric and graph conditions under which it holds.
For degree k greater than three, deleting k-2 incident edges leaves degree two; if the intended cap is three the count should be k-3.
The component-balance summation leaves the pair index domain and double-counting convention undefined.
A spanning tree changes relay routes but does not by itself enlarge each repeater's user coverage disk, contrary to parts of the explanation.
A node with multiple route neighbors may face incompatible receiver-frequency requirements; direction and duplex constraints are not formalized.
The weather-based reduction from 85.45 to 40 miles is qualitative and unsupported by attenuation data or a revised link budget.
The sentence using R at least Phi as the threshold for any two repeaters to interfere conflicts with the earlier diameter condition R at least 2 Phi.
The eleven-site construction is displayed numerically but the proof does not independently verify every point of the target disk is covered by the listed coordinates.
The optimality proof depends on the exact scope and correctness of cited Theorem r(n) for closed congruent circles.
The 104-site result does not report its maximum enclosing-circle radius, maximum cell load, or an executable constraint audit.
The 90.71 percent Monte Carlo estimate gives no random seed or confidence interval; an approximate 95 percent sampling margin is about 0.18 percentage points.
The 6.4 paragraph refers to a solution in subsection 6.4 itself, likely an erroneous self-reference to subsection 6.2.
Two examples do not establish that adding repeaters generally increases every user's reachable area under the route assignment.
Tables 6 and 8 provide coordinates and channel labels but no machine-checkable proof that every interference and directed-connectivity constraint holds.
Equation 18 gives a parameter-based transition near N=816 with the appendix values, so 'about 1000' is only a coarse description.
Figure 13 lacks independent-run variability, optimum baselines, and uncertainty for the randomized proposed algorithm.
The text calls X Bernoulli, but the displayed count distribution is binomial.
Normalizing each Figure 14 curve by its own maximum hides absolute repeater-count differences.
The two-standard-deviation capacity rule is heuristic and does not specify a target tail probability or simultaneous-overload guarantee.
Approximating the binomial standard deviation by the square root of the mean omits the one-minus-p factor.
A two-meter wavelength alone does not justify a strong general claim that VHF readily bypasses small mountains.
Figure 15 is separated from its caption across a page break and lacks a complete legend.
Multiple lower-tier repeaters sharing one transmit frequency and PL tone can collide on simultaneous uplinks without scheduling or capture assumptions.
Terrain shielding is proposed without path profiles, diffraction calculations, or link-budget validation.
The claim that the method is much faster than simulated annealing is unsupported by runtime tables or experimental settings.
The claim of higher local-optimum escape ability is unsupported by repeated-run success statistics.
The 97.12 percent reachability result is empirical and cannot replace the strong solution's universal reachability condition.
Appendix A leaves the information bit-rate parameter without a numerical value, even though it is needed in the printed capacity derivation.
The symbol table gives V_u and V_u-prime the same description, obscuring their intended difference.
Assumption A5 of no background noise conflicts directly with the use of SNR, N_0, and E_b/N_0.
Assumption A6 about no noisy impact from repeaters is poorly reconciled with I_other, I_self, and the explicit interference condition.
Treating fog, rivers, hills, buildings, and solar activity as one generic interference class mixes propagation loss, obstruction, noise, and fading.
Wikipedia and old web pages support important engineering statements but are unstable or weak primary evidence.
The paper provides no source code, random seeds, machine-readable tables, or complete reproduction package.
